inputs.original_text: Harry Wait was rightly found guilty of seeking ballots for Robin Vos and Cory Mason without their consent. That is a serious breach of the rules and of voters’ trust. But officials shouldn’t use one man’s misconduct as a shield against legitimate questions about election security. A trustworthy system can withstand lawful scrutiny—and those in authority have a duty to address any real weaknesses, not dismiss concerns to protect their own standing.
inputs.modified_text: Harry Wait was rightly found guilty of seeking ballots for Robin Vos and Cory Mason without their consent. That kind of misconduct violates the law and the basic trust elections depend on. But officials must not hide behind his case to shut down legitimate questions about election security. Lawful scrutiny is not an attack on order; it is how authorities prove they deserve the public’s confidence. If there are real weaknesses, those in charge have a duty to address them—not dismiss concerns to protect their own standing.
